details.airportInfo: Heathrow is the usual gateway for international visitors to Oxford. Direct coaches run from the airport to Oxford's city centre in roughly an hour and a half.
details.funFact: Oxford has no single campus: its colleges and university buildings are woven through the medieval city centre, so the Radcliffe Camera, the Sheldonian and the Divinity School all sit within a few minutes' walk of each other.
details.languageInfo: Oxford has its own vocabulary: terms are called Michaelmas, Hilary and Trinity, and the Radcliffe Camera is simply the 'Rad Cam'.
details.transportationFact: The historic centre is compact and best explored on foot. Bicycles are everywhere, and city buses connect the centre with the railway station and outlying colleges.

buildings.name: Radcliffe Camera
buildings.description: James Gibbs's great domed rotunda stands alone in the middle of Radcliffe Square, which is why it has become the symbol of Oxford itself. Built to house a library funded by the physician John Radcliffe, it is now a reading room of the Bodleian.

buildings.name: Sheldonian Theatre
buildings.description: Christopher Wren based his design on the open-air Theatre of Marcellus in Rome, then solved the problem of a 70-foot roof span with an ingenious timber truss. Inside, a painted ceiling shows Truth descending on the Arts and Sciences.

buildings.name: Divinity School
buildings.description: Begun in 1427, this is the oldest surviving building made for university use. Its stone ceiling is a showpiece of Perpendicular Gothic, an intricate lierne vault studded with 455 carved bosses.

buildings.name: Tom Tower
buildings.description: Wren completed Cardinal Wolsey's unfinished gatehouse at Christ Church in 1681–82, choosing a Gothic style to match the founder's work at a time when nobody was building Gothic. Its ogee dome houses Great Tom, the six-ton bell that gives the tower its name.
buildings.newUse: Christ Church gate tower and belfry

buildings.name: Clarendon Building
buildings.description: Nicholas Hawksmoor's temple-fronted building on Broad Street was finished in 1715 next to the Sheldonian and the Bodleian. Its grand portico and rooftop statues make it one of the most monumental pieces of the university's ceremonial heart.

buildings.name: Bridge of Sighs
buildings.description: Officially Hertford Bridge, this enclosed skyway links the Old and New Quadrangles of Hertford College over New College Lane. Designed by Sir Thomas Jackson and finished in 1914, it is nicknamed for its supposed likeness to the bridge in Venice.

buildings.wiki: Oxford University Museum of Natural History
buildings.name: Oxford University Museum of Natural History
buildings.description: A neo-Gothic cathedral of science, shaped by the ideas of John Ruskin. A glass roof on cast-iron columns covers the central court, and each stone column in the arcades is cut from a different British rock.
buildings.architect: Thomas Newenham Deane and Benjamin Woodward

buildings.name: Magdalen Tower
buildings.description: The bell tower of Magdalen College rises 44 metres over the High Street and the River Cherwell. It is the central focus of Oxford's May Morning celebrations each spring.

details.airportInfo: Stansted is the closest major airport to Cambridge, with direct trains to Cambridge station. Many international visitors also arrive via Heathrow or Gatwick and travel up through London.
details.funFact: The Mathematical Bridge looks like an arch but is built entirely of straight timbers, and the University Library's tower stands taller than the peak of King's College Chapel.
details.languageInfo: Cambridge students speak of 'the Backs' (the college lawns along the river), 'supervisions' (small-group teaching) and 'the UL' for the University Library.
details.transportationFact: Central Cambridge is small and flat, so most people walk or cycle. Punting along the River Cam past the Backs is the classic way to see the colleges from the water.

buildings.name: King's College Chapel
buildings.description: Built in phases from 1448 to 1515 by a succession of English kings, the chapel is one of the finest works of Perpendicular Gothic and has the world's largest fan vault. Its great windows of Flemish stained glass date from 1515 to 1531.
buildings.architect: Reginald Ely, Simon Clerk and John Wastell

buildings.name: Wren Library
buildings.description: Christopher Wren raised Trinity College's library on an open colonnade above Nevile's Court, with tall windows to flood the reading room with light. Limewood carvings by Grinling Gibbons crown the bookcases, and the shelves hold treasures from Newton's own Principia to the manuscript of Winnie-the-Pooh.
buildings.address: Trinity College, Trinity Lane, Cambridge CB2 1TQ

buildings.name: Mathematical Bridge
buildings.description: This wooden footbridge at Queens' College looks like a curved arch but is made entirely of straight timbers in a clever engineering design. It has been rebuilt twice, in 1866 and 1905, always to the same plan.
buildings.address: Queens' College, Silver Street, Cambridge CB3 9ET

buildings.name: Bridge of Sighs
buildings.description: Henry Hutchinson's covered Gothic Revival bridge carries St John's College across the Cam between Third Court and New Court. Despite the name, it has little in common with its Venetian namesake beyond being covered and arched.
buildings.address: St John's College, St John's Street, Cambridge CB2 1TP

buildings.name: Senate House
buildings.description: James Gibbs's Portland stone hall on King's Parade was meant as one side of a grand quadrangle that was never finished. It is where Cambridge students formally receive their degrees.

buildings.name: Cambridge University Library
buildings.description: Giles Gilbert Scott, who also designed Bankside Power Station (now Tate Modern), gave the library a strong industrial character and a 157-foot tower. Opened in 1934, it holds around nine million items.

details.airportInfo: Edinburgh Airport is the main gateway for St Andrews, about an hour and a half away by road. By rail, the nearest station is Leuchars, a short bus or taxi ride from town.
details.funFact: Founded in 1413, St Andrews spans six centuries of architecture in one small seaside town, from the Late Gothic St Salvator's Chapel to James Stirling's Brutalist Andrew Melville Hall, designed to resemble passing ships.
details.languageInfo: English is spoken throughout; the university's Scots name is University o St Andras and its Gaelic name Oilthigh Chill Rìmhinn.
details.transportationFact: St Andrews is a small town and the university buildings are spread along its old streets, so walking is the easiest way around. Local buses link the town with Leuchars station.

buildings.name: St Salvator's Chapel
buildings.description: Founded in 1450 by Bishop James Kennedy, who is buried inside, this Late Gothic chapel is the university's main chapel. It has been refurbished in the 1680s, the 1860s and throughout the 20th century.

buildings.name: St Mary's College
buildings.description: Founded in 1538, the college keeps much of its original 16th-century north and west ranges around a quiet quad. In the quad grow a thorn tree said to have been planted by Mary, Queen of Scots, and the King James Library founded in 1612.
buildings.oldUse: College of divinity, law, medicine and arts

buildings.name: Younger Hall
buildings.description: Paul Waterhouse's graduation hall on North Street mixes Neo-Classical and Art Deco ideas. Its foyer is lined in grey and green marble, and the main hall seats almost a thousand people.

buildings.name: Andrew Melville Hall
buildings.description: James Stirling built this hall of residence from prefabricated concrete modules on a ridge above the St Andrews Links, and it looks like a fleet of passing ships. It is now Category A listed and recognised as one of Scotland's key modern buildings.

details.airportInfo: Glasgow Airport lies just west of the city, about a 20-minute drive from the West End campus. Express buses connect it with the city centre.
details.funFact: In 1870 the university left its old High Street home for a new Gothic Revival campus on Gilmorehill designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, and it brought its 17th-century Lion and Unicorn Staircase along with it.
details.languageInfo: English is spoken everywhere, often with a strong Glaswegian accent and Scots words; the main hill-top campus is known simply as Gilmorehill.
details.transportationFact: The campus sits in the West End above Kelvingrove Park. Hillhead station on the Glasgow Subway is a short walk away.

buildings.name: University of Glasgow Memorial Chapel
buildings.description: John James Burnet's Scots Gothic chapel closes the west side of the Main Building's West Quadrangle and honours the university's dead of the First World War. Inside are carvings by Archibald Dawson and ten stained-glass windows by Douglas Strachan.

buildings.name: Lion and Unicorn Staircase
buildings.description: Carved in 1690 for the university's Old College on the High Street, this stone staircase with its lion and unicorn was moved to Gilmorehill in 1870. It now leads up beside the Memorial Chapel on the west side of the Main Building.

buildings.name: Glasgow University Library
buildings.description: William Whitfield's 12-storey Brutalist tower opened in 1968 as the centrepiece of the university's 1960s expansion across Hillhead. It is a landmark of Glasgow's West End.

buildings.name: Glasgow University Union
buildings.description: At the foot of University Avenue, Alan McNaughton's Scots Baronial building has been home to one of the oldest students' unions in the UK since 1931. Its debating tradition is famous: the union founded the World Universities Debating Championships.

details.airportInfo: Edinburgh Airport is west of the city, and the Edinburgh Trams line runs from the terminal straight into the city centre.
details.funFact: The university's buildings trace Edinburgh's architectural story: Robert Adam and William Playfair's Neoclassical Old College, Playfair's neo-Gothic New College on the Mound, Scotland's first purpose-built concert hall, and a Brutalist library by Basil Spence's firm.
details.languageInfo: Edinburgh students call Teviot Row House simply 'Teviot'. The university's Gaelic name is Oilthigh Dhùn Èideann.
details.transportationFact: Most university buildings are within walking distance of the Old Town. Lothian Buses and the tram connect the city, though the hills make for good exercise.

buildings.name: Old College
buildings.description: Robert Adam designed this grand Neoclassical quadrangle on South Bridge, and William Henry Playfair completed it to a modified design in 1827; the dome came later. It now houses the School of Law and the Talbot Rice Gallery.
buildings.architect: Robert Adam and William Henry Playfair
buildings.newUse: School of Law, administration and gallery

buildings.name: McEwan Hall
buildings.description: Sir Robert Rowand Anderson's domed graduation hall, in Italian Renaissance style, was paid for by the brewer William McEwan and finished in 1897. It is Category A listed.

buildings.name: New College
buildings.description: William Henry Playfair's neo-Gothic towers on the Mound look down on Princes Street Gardens. Opened in 1846 for the Free Church of Scotland, it has been the university's School of Divinity since 1935.

buildings.name: St Cecilia's Hall
buildings.description: Completed in 1763, this was Scotland's first purpose-built concert hall. Robert Mylne gave it an oval concert room under a domed ceiling behind a plain Neoclassical front, and today it holds the university's musical instrument collection.
buildings.newUse: Concert hall and musical instrument museum

buildings.name: Teviot Row House
buildings.description: Opened in 1889, Teviot is the oldest purpose-built student union building in the world. Sydney Mitchell designed it in a turreted Scottish Baronial style on Bristo Square.

buildings.name: Edinburgh University Library
buildings.description: The eight-storey Main Library on George Square was designed by J. M. Marshall and Andrew Merrylees of Spence, Glover and Ferguson and opened in 1967. Its long horizontal bands are a fine example of Brutalist library design.

details.airportInfo: Newcastle Airport is the nearest major airport to Durham, roughly half an hour away by road. Durham is also on the East Coast Main Line, with direct trains from London and Edinburgh.
details.funFact: University College students live in Durham Castle, a Norman fortress begun in 1072 that forms a World Heritage Site with the cathedral next door. Below it, Ove Arup's Kingsgate Bridge was built in two halves that were swung across the river to meet.
details.languageInfo: Durham students belong to colleges, and the oldest, University College, is known to everyone simply as 'Castle'.
details.transportationFact: Durham's historic peninsula is small and hilly, wrapped in a loop of the River Wear. Footbridges such as Kingsgate connect it with the colleges and departments across the river.

buildings.name: Durham Castle
buildings.description: Begun in 1072 under William the Conqueror, the Norman castle was home to the prince-bishops of Durham for centuries. Since 1837 it has housed University College, and its 14th-century Great Hall is still used for meals.

buildings.name: Cosin's Library
buildings.description: Bishop John Cosin built this library on Palace Green in 1667–68 as one of the first public libraries in northern England. It still holds his collection and is owned by the university.

buildings.name: Kingsgate Bridge
buildings.description: Ove Arup personally designed this concrete footbridge, his last structure and one of his favourites. Each half was built along the riverbank and then rotated 90 degrees to meet in the middle, where a bronze joint marks the spot.

buildings.name: Dunelm House
buildings.description: Stepping down the steep bank of the River Wear, this angular concrete building has a straight staircase through all its levels, meant to feel like an interior street. Saved from demolition, it was listed in 2021 as England's foremost post-war students' union building.
buildings.architect: Architects' Co-Partnership (Richard Raines and Michael Powers)

details.airportInfo: Dublin Airport is north of the city, and express buses run from the terminals to the city centre, stopping close to Trinity's front gate.
details.funFact: Trinity's Old Library holds the 8th-century Book of Kells, and its barrel-vaulted Long Room is one of the most famous library interiors in the world.
details.languageInfo: English is the everyday language on campus, while Irish is Ireland's first official language and appears on signs; Trinity's Irish name is Coláiste na Tríonóide.
details.transportationFact: Trinity sits right in the centre of Dublin, so the campus is easy to reach on foot. Luas trams and many city bus routes stop around its edges.

buildings.wiki: The Old Library, Trinity College Dublin
buildings.name: The Old Library
buildings.description: Thomas Burgh's library was built in stages between 1709 and 1732. Its barrel-vaulted Long Room is one of the university's most iconic sights, and the building houses the Book of Kells and the Brian Boru harp.
buildings.newUse: Library and Book of Kells exhibition

buildings.name: The Campanile
buildings.description: Sir Charles Lanyon's 30-metre granite bell tower stands at the centre of Library Square and is Trinity's best-known landmark. It was donated by Archbishop Lord John Beresford and finished in 1854.

buildings.name: Museum Building
buildings.description: Deane and Woodward's palazzo, inspired by the Byzantine buildings of Venice, is covered in over 108 carved capitals. Its domed central hall makes heavy use of Irish stone, with Romanesque arches of alternating yellow and red blocks.
buildings.architect: Thomas Newenham Deane and Benjamin Woodward

buildings.name: The Printing House
buildings.description: Richard Castle's little temple, with a pedimented portico of Portland stone, was built around 1734 and is one of Dublin's earliest Palladian buildings. It housed the Dublin University Press until 1976.

buildings.name: Provost's House
buildings.description: Built in 1759 for Provost Francis Andrews, this Palladian house with its Venetian window faces Grafton Street. It is the only one of Dublin's great Georgian houses still serving its original purpose.
